# Shiny apps

To build a shiny app we must first understand how it works. A shiny app
consists of two core components: a server and a user interface (UI). In
this section, we will explain how they are connected and work together
to create the shiny app.

## The server and the UI

A shiny app can take a static dataset and make it available for the user
to explore. Depending on how you build the app, you can allow the user
to search for specific search terms, compare expression levels, or
explore interactive figures to find new genes affected in your dataset.

## :speech_balloon: Discussion activity: Title

**Time: \\3 minutes.**

Discuss with the person next to you - what kind of data do you have that
could benefit from being interactive? Do you have an idea for an app you
want to make?

## Reading task: \~4 minutes

A shiny app can get incredibly complex and consist of many
interconnected scripts. But at it's simplest, a shiny app consists of
two elements that work together.

At it's most simple, a shiny app can be one simple function. The
following code will create a shiny app (although an empty one):

```{r}
#| eval: false
app <- shiny::shinyApp(
  ui = shiny::fluidPage(),
  server = function(input, output){}
)
shiny::runApp(app)
```

The UI (short for user interface) is what we see on the screen. The code
contains information about what is shown on the page (such as plots,
buttons and images) and in what layout (organized in columns, with a
navigation bar, etc.).

The server contains information about the objects in the UI, and how the
app should respond to user input. It contains information about what
data is displayed in the plot, what happens when you press a button, and
how the app should update when specific events happen.

A major part of building a shiny app is understanding the interplay
between the UI and the server.

![A graphical representation of the interplay between the UI and the
server. From [introduction to data
science](https://bookdown.org/hneth/i2ds/shiny.html)](/images/Shiny_ui_server.png){#fig-left-join
width="90%"}

## :book: Adding elements to our UI

**Time: \\6 minutes.**

Shiny comes with a lot of options for building a user interface. Often
you can add plots directly into a Shiny interface. lets say we want to
make a graph from the classical `iris` data set and add it into our
empty app above.

```{r}
#| label: fig-iris
#| fig-cap: "Our classical iris plot"
iris_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(iris,
                             ggplot2::aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point()

iris_plot
    
```

To add this to our app, we need to tell Shiny two things: that we want a
page in our page layout, and what we want the plot to contain.

```{r}
#| eval: false
app <- shiny::shinyApp(
  ui = shiny::fluidPage(
    shiny::plotOutput(outputId = "iris_plot"
    )
  ),
  server = function(input, output){
    output$iris_plot <- shiny::renderPlot(
      iris_plot
    )
  }
)
shiny::runApp(app)

```

If we take the code above and paste it into the console, we should get
an app with the plot. We have now created content for our app!
